deep.reconstruction:
SETTING (Fig. I, previous page). Known triangle ABC with sides a=BC, b=CA, c=AB. A fourth point P has distances alpha=PA, beta=PB, gamma=PC. The six partial angles are: 1=∠PAC, 2=∠PAB, 3=∠PBA, 4=∠PBC, 5=∠PCB, 6=∠PCA. The angles at P are 𝔄=∠BPC, 𝔅=∠CPA, ℭ=∠APB. So A=1+2, B=3+4, C=5+6, and from the three small triangles 180°−𝔄=4+5, 180°−𝔅=6+1, 180°−ℭ=2+3.

Fig. II keeps the angles at P but replaces the radii alpha, beta, gamma by alpha·beta·gamma/alpha = beta·gamma, alpha·gamma and alpha·beta. This is an inversion in P followed by a scaling. By the law of cosines the new side opposite A' is sqrt(a^2 gamma^2 + a^2 beta^2 ... ) — more precisely B'C' = sqrt(alpha^2 gamma^2 + alpha^2 beta^2 − 2 alpha^2 beta gamma cos𝔄) = alpha·a. Likewise the other sides are beta·b and gamma·c. Triangle PA'B' is similar to triangle PBA, so the angle at A' is 3+6, at B' it is 2+5 and at C' it is 1+4.

The basic equations (previous page) are:
(1) 1+2+3+4+5+6 = 180°.
(2) sin1 sin3 sin5 = sin2 sin4 sin6. This is the trigonometric form of Ceva's theorem for the concurrent cevians AP, BP, CP.

DERIVATION OF (3) (begun on the previous page, finished here):
- From (1), sin(2+3+5) = sin(1+4+6).
- Multiply by sin1·sin2 and add the two equal sides of (2).
- The identity [mine, made explicit] sin(2+3)·sin(2+5) = sin2·sin(2+3+5) + sin3·sin5 (expand and use sin²2 + cos²2 = 1) and its analogue sin(1+4)·sin(1+6) = sin1·sin(1+4+6) + sin4·sin6 then give
(3) sin1·sin(2+3)·sin(2+5) = sin2·sin(1+4)·sin(1+6).

THE NINE EQUATIONS (3)–(11). By permutation, for every odd index i in {1,3,5} and even index j in {2,4,6}:
sin i · ∏_{k odd, k≠i} sin(j+k) = sin j · ∏_{l even, l≠j} sin(i+l).
The pairs are (1,2)=(3), (1,4)=(4), (1,6)=(5), (3,2)=(6), (3,4)=(7), (3,6)=(8), (5,2)=(9), (5,4)=(10), (5,6)=(11).

REWRITING. Using A=1+2, B=3+4, C=5+6 and 4+5=180°−𝔄, 6+1=180°−𝔅, 2+3=180°−ℭ, together with (1), one gets 𝔄−A=3+6, 𝔅−B=2+5, ℭ−C=1+4. The equations become sine relations among A, B, C, 𝔄, 𝔅, ℭ and the differences 𝔄−A, 𝔅−B, ℭ−C:
- (4) sin1 sinB sin𝔄 = sin4 sinA sin𝔅
- (8) sin3 sin𝔅 sinC = sin6 sinℭ sinB
- (9) sin5 sinA sinℭ = sin2 sin𝔄 sinC

Gauss notes the equations can also be read off the figures:
- (4), (8), (9) from Fig. I. Example [mine]: (4) is the law of sines in triangles PAC and PBC, giving sin1/sin𝔅 = gamma/b and sin4/sin𝔄 = gamma/a, combined with a/sinA = b/sinB.
- (3), (7), (11) from Fig. II.
- (5), (6), (10) from both figures together.

APPLICATION TO POTHENOT'S PROBLEM (resection). Here A, B, C are known and 𝔄, 𝔅, ℭ are observed at P. Each equation contains exactly two unknown partial angles whose sum is known. For example, (4) gives sin1/sin4 = sinA·sin𝔅/(sinB·sin𝔄) with 1+4 = ℭ−C. Two angles with a known sum and a known sine ratio are found by the standard device [mine]: tan((x−y)/2) = tan((x+y)/2)·(k−1)/(k+1).

'VIERECKGLEICHUNGEN'. Fig. II is a triangle with sides a·alpha, b·beta, c·gamma and opposite angles 𝔄−A, 𝔅−B, ℭ−C. So by the law of sines
sin(𝔄−A)/(a alpha) = sin(𝔅−B)/(b beta) = sin(ℭ−C)/(c gamma) = 1/t,
where t is its circumdiameter. Gauss states 1/t = (r^2−rho^2)/(2 alpha beta gamma r), with r the circumradius of ABC and rho the distance of P from the circumcentre.

[My verification:] Fig. II is the pedal triangle of P scaled by 2r. By Euler's pedal-area theorem its area is (r^2−rho^2)·[ABC] = (r^2−rho^2)·abc/(4r). Equating this to (a alpha)(b beta)(c gamma)/(2t) gives t = 2 alpha beta gamma r/(r^2−rho^2).

Hence the three signed sines must have a common sign, namely that of r^2−rho^2. Gauss calls this the criterion of the physical possibility of the data. When P lies on the circumcircle all three vanish and the resection is indeterminate (the 'dangerous circle'); this is implicit, not stated by Gauss.
errors: Eq. (11), first line: the manuscript writes sin(6+7); this must be sin(6+3) (=sin(𝔄−A)). It is a slip, since angle 7 does not exist; the rewritten form of (11) is correct.
Eq. (6), first line: the manuscript visibly corrects a digit to give sin(2+5); the final reading is correct.
The derivation tacitly assumes P inside triangle ABC (all six angles positive, 𝔄+𝔅+ℭ=360°). For P outside, the 'sign criterion' requires a signed-angle convention, which Gauss does not spell out.
On the adjoining next page, sin𝔄 = α/q (as transcribed) should be sin𝔄 = a/q; this is not on this page.
All other equations (3)–(11), both forms, and the Viereck formula check out.

results.what: Nine trigonometric identities (3)–(11) derived from the angle-sum (1) and trig-Ceva (2) via sin(j+k)sin(j+m) = sin j·sin(j+k+m) + sin k·sin m
results.modern_name: Trigonometric Ceva theorem and its consequences for a point inside a triangle (complete quadrangle angle relations)
results.usually_credited_to: Ceva (1678) for the concurrency criterion; the trig form is folklore (18th–19th c.)

results.what: Fig. II: inversion in P gives a triangle with sides a·alpha, b·beta, c·gamma and angles 𝔄−A, 𝔅−B, ℭ−C
results.modern_name: Inversion/pedal triangle (proof of Ptolemy's inequality); pedal triangle angles ∠BPC−A etc.
results.usually_credited_to: Classical; pedal-triangle angle facts are standard 19th-century geometry (e.g. Johnson, Advanced Euclidean Geometry)

results.what: Use of each identity to solve the Snellius–Pothenot resection problem (two unknown angles with known sum and known sine ratio)
results.usually_credited_to: Snellius (1617), Pothenot (1692); Gauss's own resection treatment is published in his Werke (geodesy)

results.what: sin(𝔄−A)/(a alpha) = sin(𝔅−B)/(b beta) = sin(ℭ−C)/(c gamma) = (r^2−rho^2)/(2 alpha beta gamma r), and the same-sign criterion for consistency of the observed angles
results.modern_name: Law of sines in the pedal/inversion triangle combined with Euler's pedal-triangle area theorem (power of the point)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (pedal area, often attributed to Euler/Gergonne); 'gefährlicher Kreis' discussion in geodesy

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's interest in, and solutions of, the Pothenot problem are known. The identities are trig-Ceva consequences. The closed formula linking the inversion triangle's circumdiameter to r^2−rho^2, and the sign criterion, are elegant but follow from Euler's pedal-area theorem and were standard 19th-century geometry. The page is a nice systematic treatment but not a new major result.
